questions.solution:

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__

• 
 
It means as a person's power increases, their moral sense diminishes__.

 

Hence, **option 4** is the correct choice.

questions.question: Identify the sentence without the adverbial error.

options.text: She ran the marathon fast incredibly.
She ran the marathon incredibly fast.
She ran incredibly the marathon fast.
She ran the incredibly marathon fast.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. She ran the marathon incredibly fast.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The adverbial error in the sentence is due to the incorrect placement of the adverbs "fast" and "incredibly".
 
• In English, adverbs of manner (like "fast") typically come after the main verb or the object if there is one.
 
• When using two adverbs to describe how something is done, the adverb of degree (like "incredibly") should come before the adverb of manner.

Correct sentence: *She ran the marathon incredibly fast.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Adverbs:**

 
 
• **Adverbs of Manner:** Describe how something happens (e.g., slowly, quickly).
 
• **Adverbs of Degree:** Describe the intensity or degree of an action (e.g., very, incredibly).
 
 
 
• **Adverb Placement:**
 
 
• **Example: **She ran incredibly fast.
 
• **Rule: **Place the adverb of degree before the adverb of manner for clarity and correctness.

__
 
• The phrase "played rapidly" contains an error in adverbial usage.
 
• The verb "played" generally describes a leisurely or recreational activity, and the adverb "rapidly" (which means very fast) is inappropriate here.
 
• More suitable adverbs for "played" include "well," "happily," or "enthusiastically" depending on context.
 
• Thus, the error is located in **part 1** of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Michael and Robert **played happily** in the park near the apartment."*

• **Part 3: "in the park"** correctly indicates the location where the action took place.
 
• **Part 2: "near the apartment"** correctly provides an additional location detail modifying "in the park."

questions.question:
**The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.**

Sidharth made earnest attempts / to change / for better, / but nothing happened.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **"for better". **

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

 
• The marked answer is **"for better", **which is not grammatically correct in this context.
 
• The issue lies within the usage of the phrase **"for better", **which in standard and grammatically correct English, should be **"for the better".**
 
• The phrase **"for the better" **is a common idiom in English that refers to a change resulting in a more positive outcome, improvement, or beneficial situation.
 
• The definite article **"the" **before **"better" **is necessary when speaking about general ideas of improvement.
 
• Without **"the", **the phrase **"for better" **is not grammatically correct in this context.
 
• Let's put this into the full sentence:
 
 
• "Sidharth made earnest attempts to change **for better, **but nothing happened."
 
 
 
• Here, the sentence means that Sidharth made serious efforts to change and improve, but despite his attempts, there was no result or positive outcome.
 
 
• However, as mentioned, **"for better" **is not correct in this sentence.
 
• It should be **"for the better".**
 
 
 
• Therefore, the correct sentence is:
 
 
• "Sidharth made earnest attempts to change **for the better, **but nothing happened."
 
 
 
• This sentence correctly conveys that Sidharth made genuine efforts to improve his situation — or that he attempted to make changes that would have positive effects — but despite these efforts, there was no change.

Thus, the correct answer is **"Option 2".**

questions.question:
**From the given options, identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error. **

He cannot speak Spanish because he was born and brought up in Spain.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **because he was. **

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the usage of the conjunction **'because'. **
 
• We use because to mean **'for the reason that; since.'**
 
• In the first clause of the given sentence, it is mentioned that the person cannot speak Spanish.
 
• Now, the clause after 'because' should give us the reason why he cannot speak Spanish.
 
• However, the fact that he was born and brought up in Spain cannot be the reason behind his inability to speak Spanish.
 
• The sentence intends to mean that he cannot speak Spanish** in spite of the fact** that he was born in Spain.
 
• **Hence, the correct sentence will be** - *He cannot speak Spanish **although** he was born and brought up in Spain. *

*​ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__***

__
 
• We can also use 'even though', 'despite the fact that' and 'though'. __
 
• They essentially mean the same thing.

questions.question:
**In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'.**

Teachers' Day shall be observed (1)/as non-teaching day (2)/in our campus. (3)/No Error (4)​
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** '2' i.e. error lies in part 2 of the sentence.**

• The word 'non-teaching is an adjective and this adjective is used attributively the structure for this is 'a/an/the +adjective + noun' so that's why we need to use an indefinite article before the adjective.

They know they will face / either a swift backlash / or deafening silence.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** 1) No error.** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence does not contain any grammatical errors. It is grammatically correct and effectively conveys the intended meaning.
 
 
• *"They know they will face either a swift backlash or deafening silence."*
 
 
 
• In this sentence, all parts are properly constructed and there are no grammatical inconsistencies or errors.
 
• The use of "either...or" is appropriate, and the sentence presents two possible outcomes that the subject is aware of.
 
• The conjunction "or" is correctly used to connect the two alternatives.
 
• Therefore, the correct answer is indeed **1) No error.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/9074044cf96dc1d09ca89eac99180c3d7440ade1b364d09d47931959bf693cc8.png] Confusion Points__ **

 
• In most cases, the use of **"a" or "the"** (indefinite or definite articles) depends on whether the noun is **countable **or **uncountable**, and whether we are referring to something specific. 

 
 
• For instance, in the case of the sentences**: "either a dog or a cat", "either a queen or a king", and "either a red card or a black card", all the nouns (dog, cat, queen, king, red card, black card) **are **countable **and not specific. Therefore, we require "a" before each of these nouns.
 
 
 
• In the case of '**deafening silence**', the **noun phrase** is treated as an **uncountable noun**. It refers to a specific type of silence, one that is loud in its quietness due to its impact or significance. Since '**silence**' is uncountable, we don't necessarily need to use '**a**' necessarily before it. Therefore, we can say "or deafening silence" after "either a swift backlash".
 
• Interestingly, depending upon the context and stylistic choice of the writer, one could also use '**a'** before '**deafening silence'**. Both these versions would be grammatically correct.
 
 
• "They know they will face either a swift backlash or **a deafening silence."**
 
• "They know they will face either a swift backlash or** deafening silence."**
